papers.title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
papers.abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory. Net excitatory input onto this population decreased, most strongly that from older-memory populations, which allowed inputs of older memories to drive their own neurons again. Spreading the same total synaptic change evenly across all target populations abolished this recovery. We call this mechanism reactivation-targeted pruning: plasticity is confined to one population, whose neurons lose inputs that are silent when they fire. The mechanism held under Dale's law, and depression of excitatory synapses alone, without any inhibitory plasticity, was sufficient. These findings suggest mechanistic principles underlying REM sleep's role in memory consolidation and highlight the potential for integrating human-like learning behaviors into artificial neural networks.

This mechanism held under Dale's law and required only excitatory synaptic depression, without inhibitory plasticity.

papers.title: Wild ginseng adventitious roots restore sleep homeostasis in sleep-deprived Drosophila melanogaster.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation is increasingly recognized as a major health concern and is associated with impaired physiological and neurological functions. Panax ginseng C. A. Mey. has long been used to improve sleep quality; however, the limited availability and long cultivation cycle of natural ginseng restrict its sustainable utilization. Wild ginseng adventitious roots (ADV), produced via plant tissue culture, provide a renewable source of bioactive ginsenosides, although their potential role in sleep regulation remains poorly understood. The sleep-promoting effects and safety of ADV were evaluated in a sleep deprivation-induced Drosophila melanogaster model. Sleep parameters, including total sleep duration, sleep latency, deep sleep, and sleep fragmentation, were assessed, together with addiction-like behavioral assays. Transcriptomic analysis was performed to investigate the underlying mechanisms. LC-MS/MS and bioactivity assays were conducted to identify and validate major active ginsenosides. ADV significantly improved sleep behavior in sleep-deprived flies, increasing total sleep duration and deep sleep while reducing sleep latency and sleep fragmentation, without inducing addiction-like behaviors. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that ADV modulated multiple sleep-related biological processes, particularly stress response pathway, as evidenced by altered expression of Hsp68, Hsp70Aa, Hsp70Ba, Hsp70Bb, and Hsp70Bbb. Combined with LC-MS/MS identification and biological activity comparison, ginsenosides Rc and F2 were preliminarily identified as the principal active metabolites. In the Drosophila melanogaster sleep-deprivation model, ADV treatment is associated with improvements in sleep-related behavioural parameters alongside altered expression of conserved stress-response-related biological processes. These findings support ADV as a sustainable source of bioactive ginsenosides, though the current experimental design cannot establish a strictly sleep-specific or causal mechanistic relationship.

papers.title: Slow-wave sleep selectively amplifies network signatures of the presumed epileptogenic zone in focal epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Slow-wave sleep increases interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) and seizures in focal epilepsy, but how sleep stages reshape epileptogenic tissue remains unclear. We assessed whether sleep stages selectively modulate network properties of the presumed epileptogenic zone (pEZ) relative to irritative (IZ) and non-involved (NIZ) zones. We studied 22 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy undergoing pre-surgical intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG). IED-free resting-state epochs spanned four vigilance stages: wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep stages 2 and 3, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Spectral power, functional connectivity, graph-theoretic indices, and the 1/f exponent were quantified across seven frequency bands. Sleep stage and zone interactions were tested using permutation testing. pEZ electrodes were classified using elastic net logistic regression with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. NREM3 selectively amplified within-pEZ gamma-band synchrony beyond surrounding zones (pEZ-NIZ: d=1.204, P=0.027). pEZ local efficiency and betweenness centrality rose in beta1 and gamma bands versus wakefulness. The aperiodic exponent steepened within the IZ versus NIZ during NREM3 and NREM2 (d =1.452 and 0.87, P < 0.001 and P=0.015). A three-feature classifier (NREM3 aperiodic exponent, beta2 connectivity, gamma local efficiency) localised the pEZ without ictal recordings (median AUC 0.859 pEZ vs. non-pEZ). Slow-wave sleep selectively unmasks pEZ network properties via amplified power, synchrony and hub topology. NREM3-derived multimodal features may complement conventional pre-surgical biomarkers. Prospective validation in larger cohorts is needed to determine whether these markers improve surgical planning and outcome prediction.

papers.title: Molecular clockwork hypothesis for the KaiABC circadian oscillations.
papers.abstract: When three cyanobacterial proteins-KaiA, KaiB, and KaiC-are incubated with ATP in vitro, the phosphorylation level of KaiC exhibits stable circadian oscillations. Biochemical and structural analyses have shown that KaiC's ATPase activity is crucial for these oscillations, leading to the hypothesis that ATP-consuming dynamics function as a molecular clock, determining the oscillation period of individual molecules. Moreover, these molecular clocks synchronize collectively, resulting in oscillations at the ensemble level. In this study, we develop a theoretical model to test this molecular clockwork hypothesis. Our model clarifies the relationship between the oscillation period and ATPase activity, explaining the significant changes in the period induced by amino acid substitutions near the CI-CII domain boundary of the KaiC hexamer. Furthermore, the model addresses the physical basis for temperature compensation concerning both the oscillation period and ATPase activity. Thus, the molecular clockwork perspective provides a framework for understanding the atomic design behind collective oscillations.

papers.title: Longitudinal changes in resting-state EEG eyes-closed/open delta differentiation during an Antarctic expedition.
papers.abstract: Antarctic polar night brings extreme light deprivation, prolonged isolation and severe circadian disruption, yet longitudinal resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) signatures reflecting neurophysiological alterations in this harsh environment remain poorly characterized. In this exploratory longitudinal research, resting-state EEG recordings with eyes open (EO) and eyes closed (EC) were acquired from 16 Antarctic expeditioners at four mission stages: pre-departure, pre-polar-night, early post-polar-night, and austral summer. Linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction were applied to analyze delta eyes-closed/open differentiation (the EC-EO delta log-power difference), delta sub-bands, aperiodic spectral features, entropy, EEG microstates and delta-band functional connectivity. The delta EC-EO difference exhibited consistent, progressively negative shifts in parietal, frontal, whole-brain and occipital regions across the expedition timeline, with the most pronounced shifts observed in recordings obtained during and after the polar-night period; this effect spanned all slow, mid and fast delta sub-bands. Secondary mild temporal variations were observed in aperiodic spectral metrics, occipital sample entropy and global delta connectivity, whereas EEG microstates displayed no significant longitudinal alterations. Collectively, the delta EC-EO difference emerges as a candidate EEG index of resting-state condition differentiation in the low-frequency range, pending validation in larger studies with synchronized behavioral, physiological, and environmental measures.

papers.title: Selection on PER2 Phosphorylation Regulation Underlies Atypical Mammalian Circadian Rhythms.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are fundamental biological processes that enhance survival and reproductive fitness by coordinating physiology and behavior with predictable environmental cycles. However, in some species, circadian rhythms are weakened, irregular, or even undetectable, likely reflecting evolutionary responses to extreme environments or specialized ecological niches. Nevertheless, the genetic basis of these atypical phenotypes remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the molecular evolution of 20 PER2-associated genes across 71 representative mammalian species. We identified four genes under positive selection in mammalian lineages exhibiting atypical circadian phenotypes, three of which (CDK5, CSNK1E, and GSK3B) are involved in the post-translational regulation of PER2 phosphorylation, suggesting that PER2 phosphorylation regulators may contribute to lineage-specific circadian variation. Notably, CSNK1E, a key kinase regulating PER2 phosphorylation, showed signatures of positive selection and accelerated evolution in cetaceans, which exhibit unihemispheric slow-wave sleep (USWS). In vitro assays showed that dolphin CSNK1E increased phosphorylation at the stabilizing FASP site S662 of PER2 and extended the half-life of the PER2 protein, a molecular feature closely linked to circadian oscillator amplitude and sleep regulation. Increased PER2 phosphorylation may contribute to altered sleep and locomotor activity associated with sustained wakefulness during USWS, as supported by our cellular and whole-animal assays. Consistently, zebrafish overexpressing dolphin CSNK1E exhibited elevated locomotor activity and reduced sleep duration. Overall, our findings provide evidence that evolutionary changes in PER2 phosphorylation regulation are associated with atypical circadian phenotypes and offer novel insights into the genetic mechanisms underlying circadian plasticity in mammals.

papers.title: Is cardiovascular autonomic control during the day-to-night transition dependent on dim light melatonin onset? An exploratory analysis in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: We tested whether dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) is time-aligned with the transition between biological day into night in cardiovascular autonomic control (CV onset time). We studied 10 healthy adults (4 females, age 25 ± SD 2 years) under an ultra-short semi-constant routine protocol (<8lux). Participants remained seated for 7 h until 1 h after their habitual bedtime. We collected saliva samples every 30 min and recorded R-R intervals and beat-to-beat blood pressure every hour. DLMO was defined as the interpolated time for melatonin increase over 3 pg/mL. Phase angle was defined as the time difference between DLMO and the midpoint of self-reported sleep as a measure of the alignment between sleep-wake patterns and biological circadian rhythms. CV onset time was defined using a segmental (piecewise) analysis to identify the inflection point (X0 slope) throughout the study. CV autonomic modulation was assessed using indices of heart rate and blood pressure variability. CV onset times for all indices did not differ significantly from DLMO (p > 0.05). Mean differences between DLMO and CV onset time were significantly correlated with the phase angle of entrainment (all significant, r > +0.75). Our results suggest that CV autonomic transition into biological night was not associated with DLMO, which seems to depend on the phase angle of entrainment.

ai.summary: Exploratory study in 10 healthy adults using an ultra-short semi-constant routine tested whether dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) aligns with the day-to-night transition in cardiovascular autonomic control. Cardiovascular onset times did not differ significantly from DLMO, but DLMO–CV onset differences correlated strongly with phase angle of entrainment (r > 0.75), suggesting alignment depends on entrainment phase.

papers.title: Neuroelectrophysiological correlates of extended cessation of consciousness in advanced meditators: A multimodal EEG and MEG study
papers.abstract: In some contemplative traditions, 'extended cessation' (EC) refers to a state of advanced meditation in which the meditator self-reports intentionally suppressing their own consciousness and re-emerging with a profound sense of clarity and equanimity. Here, we present the first electrophysiological study of EC, in which five meditators underwent concurrent electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) recording. EC significantly increased high-frequency global coherence in all five of the participants, yet it did not consistently affect Lempel-Ziv complexity or power across participants. Our results provide preliminary evidence that the neural signatures of EC may be distinct from other states that are characterized by a loss of consciousness, including deep sleep and anesthesia. EC may not be simply 'switching off' consciousness but rather reorganizing the neural dynamics that underlie consciousness.

ai.summary: First electrophysiological study of 'extended cessation' meditation, with five advanced meditators undergoing concurrent EEG and MEG. papers.title: Integrative transcriptomics and metabolomics reveal Cry1-associated hepatic alterations and plasma essential fatty acids as biomarkers of residual circadian disruption post-sepsis.
papers.abstract: Sepsis disrupts circadian rhythm, leaving lasting molecular traces and circadian insensitivity to jet lag even after acute phase recovery. However, the core mechanism and biomarkers of residual circadian dysfunction post-sepsis remain unclear, which hinders targeted interventions. Male mice were subjected to non-lethal LPS injection, and after 7 days of recovery, liver transcriptomics and plasma metabolomics were integrated. Behavioral, physiological, and molecular analyses were performed, with statistical tests including DESeq2, Student's t-test, MetaCycle, and ROC curve analysis. Significant transcriptomic alterations were observed, most prominently at Zeitgeber time 21. Linoleic acid (LA) and alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) were identified as sampling-time-independent candidate biomarkers associated with post-sepsis circadian disruption. Exogenous supplementation of these two fatty acids shortened male mice's rhythm re-entrainment period. This study identifies a hypothesized Cry1-essential fatty acid axis potentially contributing to post-sepsis circadian dysfunction based on multi-omics associations, providing novel biomarkers and a metabolic intervention strategy for detecting and treating circadian rhythm disorders in sepsis survivors.

papers.title: Emerging evidence suggests that circadian disruption and muscle wasting form a self-reinforcing loop.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption and skeletal muscle wasting frequently co-occur in critical illness, shift work, and aging. We propose a bidirectional self-reinforcing loop in which each process amplifies the other. Environmental disruption of the skeletal muscle clock impairs protein turnover and mitochondrial function, triggering atrophy. The resulting loss of muscle mass weakens peripheral clock output and disrupts systemic circadian rhythms. The forward arm is supported by genetic evidence, particularly from global Bmal1 knockout models and human sleep-deprivation studies. The reverse arm is supported by correlative evidence from clinical observations and disease models. Chronotherapeutic interventions targeting this loop have shown preclinical efficacy and warrant clinical translation.

Argues chronotherapeutic interventions targeting this loop show preclinical efficacy and warrant clinical translation.

papers.title: Cognitive tests of pattern separation as sleep-sensitive measures in middle-aged and older adults: An exploratory study
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are considered both a dementia risk factor and symptom. The present research aimed to identify cognitive tests sensitive to objective sleep quantity or quality, focusing on tests designed to evaluate the earliest cognitive changes in dementia. We recruited adults who were 50 years or older and remotely monitored their sleep patterns for 7 consecutive days using wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries. On day 7, participants completed different cognitive tests; the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), the Prodromal Alzheimers and Mild Cognitive Impairment battery from the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), taxing pattern separation, and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). The final sample included 34 participants (mean age: 65.56, SD: 9.57). There were significant correlations between objective sleep quantity and PVT and MST performance. MoCA scores were correlated with performance on CANTAB and MST. Objective sleep quantity predicted MST performance when controlling for age, sex, and education. Tests of pattern separation are sensitive to objective sleep quantity and early cognitive changes associated with dementia. The sensitivity of pattern separation tests to sleep should be evaluated in a larger study, aiming to identify suitable clinical trial outcome measures for sleep-promoting treatments in older adults.

papers.title: Astrocyte molecular rhythm disruption in nucleus accumbens promotes increased binge-like drinking in mice.
papers.abstract: Alcohol misuse is a leading cause of preventable death worldwide. Chronic alcohol is associated with disrupted circadian rhythms, yet molecular mechanisms linking circadian rhythm dysregulation and alcohol consumption are poorly understood. Current FDA-approved treatments for alcohol use disorder (AUD) do not target molecular rhythms or sleep-wake cycles. Mammalian circadian rhythms are regulated by transcription-translation feedback loops that regulate expression of 'clock genes' (e.g., Arntl encoding for BMAL1). Both human and rodent studies demonstrate associations between clock gene variants and changes in reward-seeking behavior. Evidence suggests astrocytes, non-neuronal brain cells with cell-autonomous rhythms, may regulate both circadian rhythms and reward. In the nucleus accumbens (NAc), a region responsible for modulating alcohol- and reward-related behavior, over 43% of the astrocyte transcriptome is expressed rhythmically. However, no studies to date have investigated roles of NAc astrocyte rhythmicity in regulating alcohol drinking. We used AAV8-Gfap-Cre to functionally ablate molecular rhythms in NAc astrocytes of BMAL1 floxed mice. Two-bottle choice (2BC), drinking-in-the-light (DIL), and drinking-in-the-dark (DID) assessed alcohol drinking. Behavioral assays included locomotor response to novelty, sucrose preference, and social interaction. Disrupting molecular clock function in NAc astrocytes increased binge-like drinking during both DIL and DID paradigms ( d = 1.44), but not with any other drinking paradigm or behavior. This study carves out a unique role for astrocytes in controlling the temporal organization of reward circuitry and susceptibility to binge-drinking. Future studies will investigate clock-controlled astrocyte mechanisms, such as glutamate uptake and ATP release, that may underlie binge-like drinking behavior.

papers.title: Circadian rhythms and sleep disturbances: a conceptual perspective with implications for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
papers.abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is a genetic disorder characterized by cyst formation, kidney enlargement, and extrarenal complications. While the role of genetic mutations in PKD1, PKD2, and other minor genes is well established, the influence of circadian rhythms and sleep disturbances on disease progression remains underexplored. The circadian timing system, coordinated by the central clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus and synchronized with peripheral clocks in the kidneys, regulates key physiological processes, including glomerular filtration rate (GFR), sodium handling, blood pressure, and hormone secretion. In ADPKD, circadian disruption driven by intrinsic molecular alterations and exacerbated by sleep disorders contributes to sympathetic nervous system activation, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) dysregulation, and elevated vasopressin levels, all of which accelerate cyst growth and hypertension. Mechanistic links also involve the activation of the mTOR pathway, impaired fatty acid oxidation, and altered gut microbiota composition. These disturbances impair kidney function and increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. Chronotherapy and targeted sleep hygiene interventions offer promising adjunctive strategies for mitigating circadian misalignment in ADPKD. Timed administration of antihypertensives, diuretics, and disease-modifying agents, such as tolvaptan, along with melatonin supplementation, structured light exposure, and optimized physical activity patterns, may enhance therapeutic efficacy and improve quality of life (QoL). Future research should prioritize longitudinal and interventional studies incorporating circadian biomarkers to evaluate the impact of aligning therapeutic interventions with biological rhythms on kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in ADPKD.

papers.title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
papers.abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.

papers.title: Feasibility of unattended in-home polysomnography in trauma-exposed Veterans with chronic nightmares.
papers.abstract: This study examined the feasibility and acceptability of unattended home polysomnography (hPSG) in trauma-exposed U.S. Veterans with chronic nightmares (N = 47). Of the scheduled studies, 41 (87.2%) were completed. Twenty-four (58.5%) tests were successful based on all pre-specified criteria. Twenty-nine (71%) had ≥4 hours of interpretable EEG. No baseline differences were found between Veterans with and without successful hPSGs. Regarding acceptability, sleep quality was rated significantly worse on the night with hPSG compared to a night without. This study observed that unattended hPSG is partially feasible and acceptable in a group of trauma-exposed Veterans; however, failure was common. Characteristics of trauma-exposed samples, such as increased sweating and sleep movements, may have contributed to these results. Tools designed to be applied independently and to endure these factors should be considered.

papers.title: De-escalating Therapy in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea After Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist-Induced Weight Loss: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Incretin-based therapies now achieve weight reduction of a magnitude previously attainable only through bariatric surgery and have demonstrated substantial reductions in the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) in adults with obesity-related obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). Sleep services are consequently managing growing numbers of patients who undergo rapid, substantial weight loss while established on positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy, and who ask whether that therapy can be stopped. No guideline addresses this question. This narrative review synthesises three literatures that have developed largely in isolation: the relationship between weight change and OSA severity, the efficacy data for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual incretin agonists in OSA, and the experimental PAP withdrawal literature. Across randomised trials and meta-analyses, there is consistent agreement that incretin therapy reduces AHI, body weight and blood pressure, with effect magnitude varying by agent, dose and baseline adiposity. There is, however, material disagreement on three questions directly relevant to de-escalation: whether the effect is wholly weight-mediated, whether AHI reduction translates into reduction in cardiovascular risk, and what proportion of patients achieve genuine disease remission as opposed to severity reduction. Approximately half of participants in the largest trial did not reach a severity threshold at which PAP would ordinarily be considered unnecessary, and withdrawal studies demonstrate recurrence of obstructive events and adverse haemodynamic change within days of stopping therapy. This review proposes a structured, reversible and documented framework for reassessment rather than ad hoc discontinuation and identifies the evidence gaps that must be closed before de-escalation can be considered evidence-based practice.

papers.title: Pharmacological inhibition of REV-ERBα ameliorates motor deficits in the 6-OHDA-lesioned mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by nigrostriatal dopaminergic (DAergic) degeneration and motor dysfunction. Many PD patients also show circadian rhythm disturbances. Increasing evidence links circadian clock dysfunction to PD pathology. REV-ERBα is a circadian nuclear receptor that regulates DAergic genes under physiological conditions. However, its role in nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) homeostasis and motor function in PD remains unclear. In this study, we found elevated Rev-erbα mRNA expression in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive neurons of the substantia nigra (SN) in a 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) mouse model of PD. To test its functional role, we assessed the acute effects of local SN microinjection of the REV-ERBα antagonist SR8278. We found that SR8278 partially recovered motor performance and improved fine motor function. These effects occurred regardless of circadian timing. SR8278 administration did not restore TH expression or tissue DA levels in the striatum and SN. However, in vivo microdialysis showed enhanced extracellular DA turnover in the striatum. Specifically, while extracellular DA metabolites level increased, basal extracellular DA levels showed no change. Together, these findings identify REV-ERBα as a potential therapeutic target that modulates extracellular nigrostriatal DA dynamics and improves motor function in PD.

papers.title: The impact of creatine on brain functions.
papers.abstract: As an endogenous compound essential for energy homeostasis, creatine holds a fundamental role in the bioenergetics of the brain, an organ with high metabolic requirements. This review provides a synthesis of current knowledge on the impact of creatine on the functions of the central nervous system (CNS). The brain, which is capable of de novo creatine synthesis, demonstrates an increase in its internal concentrations following supplementation; however, this effect is less significant than in muscle tissue and is constrained by the blood-brain barrier, among other factors. The development of effective CNS-targeted dosing strategies remains a subject of ongoing research. An overview of the literature suggests that creatine supplementation may beneficially influence cognitive performance, particularly under conditions of elevated metabolic demand like stress or sleep deprivation, with the potential to enhance memory and mitigate fatigue. Nonetheless, findings from the cited research are inconsistent due to methodological heterogeneity and a common failure to directly measure brain creatine levels. Reports on creatine's antidepressant properties are particularly encouraging, with preclinical and initial clinical studies pointing to its potential utility (e.g., via the mTORC1 pathway) in augmenting mood disorder treatments. papers.title: TCANet: a temporal convolutional attention network for EEG-based cognitive load assessment in simulated flight tasks.
papers.abstract: Effective cognitive load assessment facilitates optimized task allocation and plays a critical role in evaluating human performance in domains such as flight safety monitoring and human-computer interaction. Electroencephalography (EEG) has been extensively employed in cognitive load research owing to its high temporal resolution, non-invasiveness, and accessibility. However, EEG signals exhibit substantial variability across individuals and task conditions, making it challenging to extract stable and discriminative features related to cognitive load. Accordingly, we propose TCANet, a Temporal Convolutional Attention Network designed to learn discriminative EEG representations for cognitive load classification in simulated flight tasks. The proposed network integrates multi-branch temporal convolutions, dilated convolutions, and attention mechanisms to model temporal, spatial, and channel-wise EEG information while reducing redundant feature responses. We designed an EEG-based cognitive load classification paradigm involving two pilot-simulated flight scenarios. A total of 20 participants were recruited, with 15 participants completing the turning task and 5 participants completing the landing task. TCANet achieved average classification accuracies of 90.15% and 81.52% on the turning-task and landing-task datasets, respectively. The turning-task dataset served as the primary evaluation dataset, whereas the landing-task dataset provided a supplementary evaluation under a different simulated flight task. Statistical analyses of frequency-band power indicated task-condition-related variations in EEG spectral activity. Neurophysiological variations, particularly in the Theta and Alpha bands, and feature representation analyses further provided interpretable evidence regarding cognitive-load-related EEG patterns and the discriminative representations learned by TCANet.

papers.title: Digital behavior therapy for insomnia in the general population: secondary analysis of the multi-arm RESiLIENT trial with active comparators.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is common and often coexists with depression and anxiety. Digital delivery can expand access, yet few trials have compared insomnia-focused behavioral interventions with strong active controls under standardized conditions. To examine whether a smartphone-delivered behavior therapy for insomnia (BI) improves insomnia more than a mood-focused behavioral activation (BA) module or a health-information (HI) comparator, and whether combining BI with BA (BA+BI) adds benefit. We conducted a secondary analysis of the multi-arm RESiLIENT randomized controlled trial among adults from the general population with elevated insomnia (Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) ≥8). Participants were assigned to BI, BA+BI, BA, or HI, each self-guided over six weeks. The primary outcome was ISI change at weeks 6 and 26, analyzed using mixed-effects models. Depressive (PHQ-9) and anxiety (GAD-7) symptoms were secondary outcomes. Analyses followed a modified intention-to-treat approach (≥1 post-baseline assessment). At week 6, BI reduced insomnia severity more than HI (ES: -0.43, CI: -0.58 to -0.28) and BA (ES: -0.26, CI: -0.42 to -0.11); BA also exceeded HI (ES: -0.16, CI: -0.32 to -0.01). Adding BA to BI gave no benefit over BI alone (vs HI, ES: -0.30, CI: -0.45 to -0.14). BI reduced depressive (ES: -0.44, CI: -0.59 to -0.29) and anxiety symptoms (ES: -0.27, CI: -0.42 to -0.12) more than HI, and matched BA (each ES: 0.05, CI: -0.10 to 0.20). At week 26, ISI differences persisted but PHQ-9 and GAD-7 differences attenuated. This exploratory, hypothesis-generating analysis associated a focused smartphone-delivered sleep intervention with durable improvements in insomnia severity and mood. Replication in independent samples, and confirmation in trials recruiting participants with elevated insomnia, is required before recommendation at scale.

papers.title: A sliding window and Fourier decomposition method based 1D-CNN framework for motor imagery EEG classification.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signal classification is fundamental requirement for effective motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. However, current MI classification methods often depend on handcrafted spatial filtering or complex time-frequency transformations that increase computational complexity. To mitigate this limitation, we propose a unified architecture that integrates a sliding window (SW), a Fourier decomposition method (FDM), and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) for MI-EEG classification. The raw EEG data were segmented using the SW approach to augment the data and extract more temporal feature patterns from each trial. The segmented signal, containing time-domain features, was subsequently processed using a band-pass filter and FDM to extract frequency-based features. Here, FDM decomposes the signal into eight orthogonal Fourier Intrinsic Band Functions (FIBFs). A 1D-CNN architecture was employed to learn representations from the decomposed EEG signals. The proposed framework was evaluated on the BCI Competition III Dataset IVa (BCIC III IVa) and BCI Competition IV-2a (BCIC IV 2a) datasets. Our method achieved accuracies of 79.14% and 93.67% on the BCIC IV 2a and BCIC III IVa datasets, respectively, under the subject-dependent evaluation protocol. To evaluate cross-subject generalization, the proposed framework was validated using the Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) protocol, achieving average classification accuracies of 76.49% on the BCIC III Dataset IVa and 55.50% on the BCIC IV 2a dataset. Furthermore, deployment on the NVIDIA Jetson Nano demonstrated complete pipeline latencies of 58.119 ms/trial and 85.055 ms/trial, corresponding to throughputs of 17.21 and 11.76 trials/s for the BCIC III IVa and BCIC IV 2a datasets, respectively. The results show the strong potential of the developed MI-EEG classification method to assist subjects with motor ailments.

papers.title: A novel age-based physiological definition of adherence to pediatric long-term non-invasive ventilation: an exploratory study.
papers.abstract: The indications for pediatric long-term non-invasive ventilation (LT-NIV) have expanded. However, a standardized definition of pediatric adherence is lacking. To propose a novel physiological definition of adherence to pediatric LT-NIV and compare it with the two commonly used adult-derived definitions. Retrospective cross-sectional study including all eligible children aged 0.15-18 years enrolled in the LT-NIV follow-up program at Hospital Garrahan, Argentina. Clinical data were obtained from medical records and adherence from device memory downloads. The proposed definition classified patients as "adherent" when LT-NIV use reached ≥ 70% of the minimum age-specific recommended sleep duration (American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus) on ≥ 70% of nights, replacing a fixed threshold with one tailored to each child´s sleep needs. This was compared to the current(≥ 4 h/night on ≥ 70% of nights) and classic (≥ 4 h/night on ≥ 50% of nights) adult-derived definitions. Eighty patients were included (median age 9.01years, IQR 5.96-14.09). The most frequent diagnoses were neuromuscular (31%) and genetic disorders (15%). LT-NIV was initiated electively in 91%, 75% reported sleep-disordered breathing symptoms, polysomnography was abnormal in 95.2%. Adherence rates were 66.25% (novel definition); 83.75% (classic definition) and 78.75% (current definition), p = 0.0005 and p = 0.0039 respectively. Poorer adherence was associated with younger age, developmental delay, absence of symptoms, earlier ventilation initiation and lower pressure settings. Our results highlight an overestimation of adherence when adult definitions are used. This first study explores a novel pediatric adherence definition for LT-NIV. Our research calls for action to discuss new international pediatric adherence thresholds.

papers.title: The effects of multiregional fascial mobilization on heart rate and physiological parameters in patients with obstructive sleep apnea: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with increased sympathetic activity and an elevated cardiovascular risk. Noninvasive interventions targeting autonomic regulation may offer complementary therapeutic strategies. This randomized controlled trial aimed to investigate the acute effects of multiregional fascial mobilization on the physiological parameters of patients with OSA. Patients with polysomnography-confirmed moderate-to-severe OSA (apnea-hypopnea index ≥ 15 events/hour) were randomly assigned to an intervention group that received a standardized 16-minute multiregional fascial mobilization protocol or a control group that rested quietly in the supine position for the corresponding period without receiving manual or tactile intervention. The intervention targeted the cervical, thoracic, and abdominal regions, under controlled conditions. The primary outcomes included heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and peripheral oxygen saturation. Measurements were obtained at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and 5 and 15 minutes post-intervention. A total of 95 male patients (mean age: 48.12 ± 10.21 years) completed the study. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the groups, except for heart rate. After adjustment for baseline heart rate using mixed analysis of covariance, no significant group × time interaction was observed for heart rate (P = .476, partial ηp2 = .008). Similarly, no significant group × time interactions were observed for systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, or peripheral oxygen saturation (all P > .05). Although significant time effects were observed for some physiological parameters, the magnitude of these effects varied across outcomes, and none was accompanied by a significant group × time interaction. Therefore, these temporal changes were not interpreted as intervention-specific effects. No adverse events were reported. Heart rate changed significantly over time following the interventions; however, after adjustment for baseline heart rate, the pattern of change did not differ significantly between the fascial mobilization and control groups. Similarly, no significant between-group differences in changes over time were observed for blood pressure or oxygen saturation. These findings do not demonstrate a specific acute effect of multiregional fascial mobilization on the physiological parameters assessed. Further studies using advanced measures of autonomic function and longer follow-up periods are warranted.

papers.title: Effects of West Nile Virus on behavioral and cognitive performance, circadian body temperatures, cortical Aβ and p-tau pathology, and immune measures in human apoE and human amyloid precursor protein NL-G-F/human apoE mice.
papers.abstract: There are three human apolipoprotein E (E) isoforms: E2, E3, and E4. Compared with E3, E4 is an AD risk factor. West Nile Virus (WNV) can cause neurological disease, and it results in some neuropathology and neuroinflammation seen in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Previously, we reported on the effects of exposure to the Kunjin strain (KUNV) of WNV in middle-aged knock-in (KI) mice expressing human amyloid precursor protein (APP) containing the dominant NL-G-F mutations with human apoE targeted replacement (TR) mice on behavioral, immune, and pathological measures, and circadian body temperatures. NL-G-F/E4 mice were more susceptible to KUNV-induced cognitive injury and prolonged viral load in the cortex; viral load was detected in the cortex of more mice expressing amyloid precursor protein with the dominant NL-G-F AD mutations and expressing also E4 than those expressing also E3. As NL-G-F and NL-G-F/apoE mice show cognitive injury and neuropathology at 6 months of age and age is a risk factor to develop AD and modulates the immune response in AD, we assessed in this study whether genotype differences in response to KUNV exposure are seen in younger mice. To determine whether the presence of NL-G-F is required to detect genotype differences in response to KUNV and/or modulates the response to KUNV, E3 and E4 mice were included as well. As compared with E3, E2 reduces the risk to develop AD and the vast majority of AD would likely not occur in the absence of E3 and E4 NL-G-F/E2 mice were included in this study as well. We crossed knock-in (KI) mice expressing human amyloid precursor protein (APP) containing the dominant NL-G-F mutations with human apoE targeted replacement (TR) mice and used middle-aged NL-G-F/E3 and NL-G-F/E4 mice to assess the role of WNV (subtype Kunjin virus) (KUNV) exposure on behavioral alteration performance, circadian body temperatures, viral loads, neuropathology, and transcript levels of three immune measures in cortex important in the detrimental effects of KUNV on brain function. There were apoE isoform-dependent responses to KUNV exposure on various measures already seen at 6 months of age and are mostly more profound in the absence than in the presence of NL-G-F. One week following exposure, cortical insoluble p-tau levels were lower in KUNV- than PBS-treated apoE, but not NL-G-F/apoE mice. Soluble p-tau levels in cortex were higher in KUNV- than PBS-treated mice, and this effect was more pronounced in NL-G-F/apoE than apoE mice. The insoluble/soluble p-tau ratio was lower in KUNV- than PBS-treated mice, and this effect was more pronounced in apoE than NL-G-F/apoE. These results are consistent with results in cultured cells supporting that Aβ and p-tau might have antiviral properties.

papers.title: A Reproducible Safety Assessment Model for Concurrent Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation with Implanted Intracranial Electroencephalography Electrodes.
papers.abstract: Concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation and intracranial EEG (TMS-sEEG) offers a powerful approach for interrogating human brain circuits with high spatiotemporal resolution. However, standardized safety testing procedures for TMS in the presence of implanted electrodes are lacking. To establish and validate a reproducible methodological framework for assessing TMS safety with sEEG hardware, addressing potential risks of electrode displacement, heating, and secondary current induction. A conductive agarose phantom implanted with clinical-grade platinum sEEG electrodes was exposed to single-pulse TMS (0.4 Hz), repetitive TMS (1-50 Hz), and intermittent theta burst stimulation. Electrode displacement was quantified via high-speed video and motion tracking. Temperature changes were measured with fiber-optic thermal probes positioned at stimulated electrode contacts. Induced voltages were recorded using an oscilloscope and intracranial EEG hardware, and secondary current and charge density were calculated from oscilloscope outputs and impedance measurements. sEEG lead displacement remained micrometer-scale across stimulation conditions, with a maximum transient displacement of 10.99 μm and a maximum 1-s mean displacement from the pre-TMS position of 16.27 μm. Temperature changes remained well within the 2°C safety threshold across all tested conditions; in the primary temperature series, the maximum observed increase was 0.073°C. Induced voltages and charge densities remained below established safety limits, exhibiting consistent exponential decay with increasing distance from the coil. All stimulation conditions, including those exceeding typical clinical ranges, remained well within safety margins. Under the tested conditions in a controlled phantom environment, TMS exposure produced micrometer-scale transient and longer-timescale displacement, temperature changes within established safety thresholds, and charge densities within established safety thresholds. This validated methodological pipeline provides a standardized framework for future safety experiments involving TMS and implanted devices and supports continued development of TMS-sEEG as a tool for studying human brain circuitry and neuromodulation.

papers.title: Electroencephalography Changes in Emotional Recognition: A Signal Processing Approach Using Wavelet Features.

EEG signal variations associated with emotional states can be analysed using wavelet-based signal processing within the arousal-valence framework. This study aims to analyse EEG signal variations associated with emotional states using a wavelet-based signal processing approach within the arousal-valence framework. A prospective observational study was conducted on 48 healthy participants. Emotional states were induced using image, video and music stimuli categorised under the arousal-valence model. EEG signals were recorded using the standard 10-20 electrode placement system. The acquired signals were pre-processed and analysed using discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to extract time-frequency features, including energy and entropy. Statistical analysis was performed to evaluate hemispheric differences and gender-based variations. Differences in EEG activity were observed between the left and right hemispheres across multiple emotional states (p < .05). Video and music stimuli produced stronger and more distinguishable EEG responses compared to image-based stimuli. Negative emotions demonstrated higher discriminative patterns than positive emotions. Gender-based variations were also observed in EEG responses. Wavelet-based EEG feature analysis provides meaningful and discriminative information for emotion recognition and may provide a robust feature set for future machine learning-based emotion recognition systems. Further studies incorporating classification algorithms and larger data sets are required to validate their predictive performance.

papers.title: Multiscale neural signatures of long-lag repetition learning: a simultaneous fNIRS-EEG study.
papers.abstract: Repetition-based learning supports word recognition and reading fluency, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly where deficits in consolidating repeated linguistic input may underlie reading and language difficulties. Establishing reliable neural markers of repetition-based learning is a critical first step toward characterizing the phenotypes of these difficulties in children. We developed a whole-brain simultaneous functional near-infrared spectroscopy-electroencephalography (fNIRS-EEG) approach to capture fast temporal electrophysiological and spatially accurate hemodynamic signals during long-lag repetition learning. Thirty participants performed a semantic judgment task with words repeated across four runs with intervening items, modeling repetition demands central to reading instruction. A multimodal decoding framework integrating electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and cross-modal fNIRS-EEG correlation features was used to classify repetition-based learning. Repeated words showed response time reductions. EEG captured a frontal N400-range repetition-related negativity and attenuation of alpha-beta suppression, reflecting changes in recognition-related and post-recognition processing. fNIRS revealed left inferior frontal and superior temporal efficiency increases alongside right supramarginal activation, suggesting integrative processing. Multimodal classifiers outperformed unimodal classifiers, indicating that each modality captured complementary aspects of learning. Combining fNIRS and EEG with multimodal machine learning provides a richer characterization of repetition-based learning than either modality alone, establishing a framework for phenotyping language learning capacity and identifying neural markers of reading difficulties in pediatric populations.

papers.title: Beyond a Single Hypoxic Burden Value: Hypoxic Burden Ratio Assessed by Peripheral Arterial Tonometry in Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: Hypoxic burden (HB) integrates the depth and duration of nocturnal oxygen desaturation in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but a single HB value may conceal distinct hypoxemic profiles. We explored the relationship between two automated HB measures derived from peripheral arterial tonometry-based home sleep apnea testing (PAT-HSAT) data: desaturation area under the SpO2 baseline (HB_baseline) and area under 90% SpO2 (HB_<90%). We performed a retrospective cross-sectional study of 2136 adults with OSA, diagnosed by a peripheral arterial tonometry-derived apnea-hypopnea index based on 3% desaturation criteria (pAHI3%) ≥5 events/h. Three operational HB groups were designated according to the relationship between HB_baseline and HB_<90%. Type 1 was characterized by measurable HB_baseline (>0%·min/h) and HB_<90% = 0%·min/h; the HB_baseline/HB_<90% ratio was not calculable because the denominator was zero. Among patients with measurable HB_<90%, Type 2 was defined by an HB ratio ≥1 and Type 3 by an HB ratio <1. These three groups were prespecified as exploratory operational categories. Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 comprised 506 (23.7%), 1108 (51.9%), and 522 (24.4%) patients, respectively. The percentage of total sleep time (TST) with SpO2 below 90% (T90) had median values of 0.1%, 5.4%, and 63.6% in Types 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Types 2 and 3 had similar median pAHI3% (26.3 and 28.8 events/h) but markedly different median HB_<90% (6.0 and 86.5%·min/h). HB_baseline correlated strongly with pAHI3% across all groups (Spearman ρ, 0.9295-0.9378), whereas HB_<90% correlated moderately with pAHI3% in Types 2 and 3 (ρ=0.6292 and 0.6209; all P<0.001). The relative magnitude of HB_baseline and HB_<90% provides an exploratory operational framework for describing distinct hypoxemic profiles in OSA beyond a single HB value. The framework is descriptive and hypothesis-generating; its clinical, prognostic, mechanistic, and therapeutic utility has not been established and requires external and longitudinal validation.

papers.title: Differential Cerebral Perfusion Patterns Across Migraine Phenotypes: An Exploratory ASL MRI Study.

The final cohort comprised 143 patients with migraine and 49 healthy controls who underwent three-dimensional pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (ASL) MRI. Voxel-wise analyses of normalized CBF (nCBF) were performed to identify phenotype-related perfusion alterations. Sensitivity analyses repeated the voxel-wise comparisons with phenotype-appropriate clinical covariates. Exploratory correlation analyses examined associations between regional perfusion and clinical characteristics. Logistic regression was further used to assess whether perfusion measures provided additional information for differentiating migraine with aura (MA) from migraine without aura (MO). Compared with healthy controls, migraine patients with depressive symptoms showed reduced nCBF in a right hippocampus-parahippocampal cluster (Cluster 1) in the primary voxel-wise analysis; however, this finding did not survive additional adjustment for sleep quality. Lower Cluster 1 nCBF was associated with greater headache frequency. Compared with MO, patients with MA showed increased nCBF in a right cerebellar-occipitotemporal cluster peaking in the right cerebellar Crus I (Cluster 2), and this difference remained significant after additional adjustment for sleep quality, medication-overuse headache status, and preventive medication exposure. Within the MA group, higher Cluster 2 nCBF was associated with greater headache intensity. In exploratory logistic regression analysis, the combined clinical-imaging model showed a higher apparent area under the curve (AUC) than the clinical model alone. These findings highlight the importance of considering clinical heterogeneity in migraine neuroimaging and suggest that ASL-derived perfusion measures may provide complementary biological information for phenotype characterization, particularly with respect to aura status.

papers.title: Acute Psychosis and Dissociative Syndrome Following Binge Recreational Nitrous Oxide Use: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Recreational nitrous oxide (N2O) inhalation is increasingly prevalent among young adults, but acute psychiatric presentations following short-term binge exposure remain poorly characterized. We report a case of a female in her early 20s with no prior history of psychotic illness who developed an acute psychotic and dissociative syndrome over three days at an outdoor music festival. Her presentation followed heavy recreational N2O and 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) exposure combined with sleep deprivation. On admission, she exhibited profound disorientation, inability to recognize close family members, polymorphic delusions, passivity phenomena, and auditory and olfactory hallucinations, requiring involuntary psychiatric hospitalization. Diagnostic workup revealed normal brain and cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a normal electroencephalogram (EEG) without epileptiform activity or slowing. Serum homocysteine was moderately elevated (25.2 µmol/L) alongside a low-normal vitamin B12 concentration (270 pg/mL), consistent with N2O-induced functional cobalamin deficiency; both markers normalized following parenteral vitamin B12 and oral folic acid supplementation. During inpatient stay, treatment with risperidone was followed by progressive neutropenia, which fully resolved after cross-titration to aripiprazole. She gradually regained full insight, was discharged on day 12, and remained free of psychotic symptoms at her three-week outpatient review. This case suggests that short-term binge N2O exposure, together with MDMA and sleep deprivation, may contribute to severe neuropsychiatric presentations without chronic use; it illustrates the value of measuring homocysteine rather than relying solely on serum B12 levels; and highlights potential hematological adverse effects during antipsychotic initiation.

papers.title: Pancreatic hamartoma presenting with sleep-related behavioral abnormalities due to neuroglycopenia: a case report.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic hamartoma (PH) is an exceedingly rare benign non-neoplastic lesion of the pancreas. Owing to its nonspecific clinical and radiological features, it is prone to misdiagnosis. Among its various subtypes, functionally active pancreatic hamartomas with distinct endocrine activity have only been sporadically reported in the literature as individual cases. We report the case of a 58-year-old female patient whose initial presentation was characterized by paroxysmal behavioral abnormalities during nocturnal sleep, manifesting as sudden agitation, arm-flinging, and purposeless stereotyped movements after sleep onset. During these episodes, the patient exhibited a confusional state with subsequent complete amnesia for the events, a clinical phenotype highly suggestive of REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) or frontal lobe epilepsy. In-hospital monitoring revealed refractory nocturnal hypoglycemia. Imaging studies identified a mass in the pancreatic tail, and the patient underwent laparoscopic distal pancreatectomy. Postoperative histopathological and immunohistochemical examination confirmed the diagnosis of pancreatic hamartoma, composed predominantly of islet cells (approximately 90%) with associated islet cell tumor-like hyperplasia. Following surgery, the patient's nocturnal hypoglycemia and sleep-related behavioral abnormalities resolved completely.

In this double-blind, randomized, controlled trial, elderly patients were randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to receive multiple low-dose intranasal dexmedetomidine administration (MD group) or normal saline nasal spray (NS group). The primary outcome was the incidence of PPCs within 7 days after surgery. Key secondary outcomes included the severity grading and classification of PPCs. Other secondary outcomes included serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) levels, Richards-Campbell sleep questionnaire (RCSQ) scores at predefined time points, and adverse reactions. A total of 190 patients were screened, and 186 completed the study. The incidence of PPCs was significantly lower in the MD group than in the NS group (9.68% vs. 22.58%, P = 0.017), with a risk ratio (RR) of 2.333 [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.173-6.317], absolute risk reduction (ARR) of 12.90%, and number needed to treat (NNT) of 7.75. After Bonferroni correction, the between-group difference in PPCs severity grading was not statistically significant (corrected P = 0.072). papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Integrated Chinese and Western Medicine for Depression With Anxiety and Somatic Symptoms: A Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveSomatic symptoms are often linked with depression and anxiety, making diagnosis difficult and limiting treatment effectiveness. Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine has been studied as a complementary approach; however, its efficacy and safety have not been systematically evaluated. This review and meta-analysis examined the effectiveness and safety of integrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine in patients diagnosed with depression with or without comorbid anxiety and somatic symptoms.MethodsThis systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. English-language studies published from 2014 to 2026 were searched in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. Randomized controlled trials comparing integrated therapy with control interventions were included. The primary outcome was depression severity assessed by HAMD scores. Secondary outcomes included anxiety symptoms, somatic symptoms, and adverse events. A random-effects model was used, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic.ResultsEleven studies met review criteria. Integrated therapy significantly reduced depression severity compared with the standard Western medicine control condition (MD = -3.95, 95% CI: -4.71 to -3.19; I2 = 59%). Anxiety symptoms were also significantly reduced (MD = -3.95, 95% CI: -4.65 to -3.26; I2 = 50%). Somatic symptoms, including sleep disturbances and pain-related outcomes, improved but were assessed descriptively because of reporting variability. Adverse events were lower or similar in combined treatment groups, indicating a favorable safety profile. Funnel plot analysis suggested minimal publication bias.ConclusionIntegrated Traditional Chinese and Western medicine was associated with greater improvements in depression and anxiety symptoms than the included control interventions, which comprised Western medicine alone, placebo/sham interventions, or usual care, while showing generally good tolerability. However, given the methodological limitations, heterogeneity of comparator conditions, and low certainty of the available evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

papers.title: Interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention: EEG evidence for joint modulation of late perceptual processing.
papers.abstract: Voluntary action shapes our perception through sensory predictions of its consequences. These predictions are thought to inhibit perceptual processing of predicted outcomes, leading to sensory attenuation. However, some studies have reported findings that contrast with this effect, suggesting that the influence of predictions may reflect, or interact with, attentional processes. Here, we investigated the interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention on early and late perceptual processing, with prediction and attention referring to the likelihood of a sensory event and its behavioral relevance, respectively. Electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded while participants viewed two sequential gratings. The orientation of the first was either predicted and self-generated or unpredicted and externally generated. Participants judged the tilt direction of the second grating relative to the first but responded only when the grating appeared in a task-relevant color. EEG analyses revealed no modulation of early visual potentials (N1a), but modulations at later processing stages. Specifically, the P3b exhibited reduced amplitude for predicted compared to unpredicted stimuli, but only when they were task-relevant, whereas task-relevance enhanced the P3b only for unpredicted stimuli. Interestingly, multivariate pattern analysis showed significant temporal clusters for decoding the grating's orientation exclusively for predicted and task-relevant stimuli, although decoding performance did not significantly differ between conditions. Furthermore, predicted and task-relevant stimuli elicited faster behavioral responses, with prediction-related P3b latency differences correlating with reaction-time differences. Overall, converging findings from the P3b, multivariate, time-frequency and behavioral analyses provide suggestive evidence that top-down attention and action-based prediction may jointly facilitate late perceptual and decision-related processing.

papers.title: Cannabidiol (CBD) for Pain: A Narrative Review of Evidence to Date.
papers.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD), the principal non-intoxicating phytocannabinoid of Cannabis sativa, is widely marketed and self-administered for pain relief, yet its regulatory status as an analgesic remains unapproved. This review synthesizes preclinical mechanistic data, human pharmacokinetic data, and clinical trial evidence across major pain conditions in order to summarize the current evidence for, or against, efficacy and safety for pain. A synthesis of published information was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, and other databases, integrating findings from systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and pharmacology reviews on CBD (independent of combination products where possible) and pain of any etiology. Preclinical and mechanistic data support plausible physical analgesic pathways for CBD, including receptor modulation, indirect enhancement of endocannabinoid tone via fatty-acid-binding-protein (FABP) inhibition, and anti-inflammatory effects. However, translation to clinical benefit has been inconsistent. In the largest meta-analysis of cannabinoids for pain, cannabinoids reduced chronic pain and improved sleep quality, but effect sizes fell below predefined minimally important clinical differences, and cannabinoids showed no benefit for acute or cancer pain, while increasing non-serious adverse events. CBD randomized trials in knee osteoarthritis, fibromyalgia, and acute low back pain have consistently failed to separate from placebo, whereas smaller/lower-quality trials and observational surveys report subjective benefit. Safety data increasingly point to dose-dependent hepatotoxicity risk. Despite strong biological plausibility and considerable consumer use, current high-quality evidence does not support CBD monotherapy as an effective analgesic across most pain conditions studied to date. Safety monitoring, particularly of liver enzymes at higher doses, is warranted.

papers.title: Seven-day Accelerometer-derived Wrist Activity after Acute Stroke Stratified by Hemiparesis Severity: A Prospective Observational Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: This hypothesis-driven prospective pilot study characterized 7-day trajectories of bilateral wrist activity after acute stroke by baseline Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE) severity. We hypothesized that mild impairment would be associated with greater paretic-side activity and more symmetric activity, whereas bilateral balance would change little despite clinical improvement. Patients who began rehabilitation within 3 days after stroke wore bilateral wrist accelerometers for 7 days. Exploratory strata were mild (FMA-UE >45) and severe (≤45), based on an inflection point of 45.3 reported for subacute stroke. Daily vector magnitude (VM) and magnitude ratio [MR = log10(paretic VM/non-paretic VM)] were analyzed using sex-adjusted linear mixed-effects models with participant random intercepts. Unannotated walking, care, therapy, and sleep were included; indices therefore represented overall inpatient wrist acceleration. Of 32 enrolled patients, 24 completed monitoring (mild impairment, n = 16; severe impairment, n = 8). At day 1, the severe group had lower paretic VM [β = -468,257 counts/day; 95% confidence interval (CI) -826,564 to -109,949; P = 0.010] and MR (β = -0.348; 95% CI -0.515 to -0.181; P <0.001) than the mild group. In the mild reference group, day coefficients were positive for non-paretic VM (β = 46,589; P <0.001) and paretic VM (β = 34,801; P = 0.002). Group-by-day interactions were nonsignificant, and MR showed no significant day effect. FMA-UE and Action Research Arm Test scores increased in both groups. Wrist activity and bilateral balance differed by baseline severity. MR showed no significant temporal change despite improved clinical motor scores. Bilateral wrist accelerometry may complement clinical assessment but reflects overall wrist acceleration rather than purposeful upper-limb use.

papers.title: Pressure Injury Prevention in Advanced Cancer: A Narrative Review and Proposed Comfort-Prioritized, Risk-Stratified Framework.
papers.abstract: Patients with advanced cancer are particularly vulnerable to pressure injury (PI) because of immobility, symptom-related positioning constraints, moisture exposure, nutritional compromise, and progressive physiological deterioration. PIs can increase symptom burden and nursing complexity and substantially impair quality of life. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on PI risk assessment tools, risk factors, and preventive strategies for adults with advanced cancer. Evidence was drawn from oncology-specific validation and observational studies, palliative care literature, international clinical guidelines, and studies involving broader high-risk populations, with the directness and certainty of evidence distinguished for major recommendations. Oncology-specific evidence supports selected risk factors and assessment approaches, whereas much of the evidence for preventive interventions is extrapolated from non-oncology populations. Pressure-redistribution support surfaces, individualized repositioning, selective preventive dressings, nutritional care, and symptom management should therefore be tailored to PI risk, intervention burden, prognosis, patient preferences, and goals of care. To integrate these considerations, we propose a comfort-prioritized, risk-stratified conceptual framework for advanced cancer care. The framework supports individualized decision-making across palliative and actively dying phases while emphasizing both PI-related and patient-centered outcomes, including comfort, pain, sleep disruption, and goal-concordant care.

papers.title: From community diagnosis to policy dialogue: co-creating childhood obesity prevention strategies in rural and urban Portugal.
papers.abstract: Promoting healthy lifestyles from early childhood is central to balanced development and the prevention of health problems throughout life. The European HEALTH4EUKids project examines a participatory process of community diagnosis, co-creation into local policies for child health promotion and childhood obesity prevention in two Portuguese territories with distinct rural and urban profiles. A cross-sectional observational study was conducted within a mixed-methods action-research framework. The study provides an exploratory assessment of children's wellbeing indicators and contextual differences, without permitting causal inference. Participants included 202 primary-school pupils (mean age = 7.43 ± 1.14 years) and 54 community adults (mean age = 48.76 ± 11.51 years), alongside stakeholders from health, community, and local decision-making sectors. Data included a questionnaire adapted from the 2022 Health Behavior in School-aged Children (HBSC) protocol, KIDSCREEN-10, the Living Healthy Tool (LHT) which was translated and culturally adapted for the Portuguese context, satisfaction questionnaires and focus groups. LHT-student version was administered exclusively in Alter do Chão. Quantitative and qualitative data were analyzed using SPSS v.28.0 and thematic analysis supported by MAXQDA. Descriptive analyses indicated that 57% of pupils reported irritability or bad mood and 46.7% reported nervousness, while quality of life and sleep were generally favorably rated. Regarding nutritional status, 66% had age-adjusted BMI within the reference range, whereas 36% reported not engaging in regular physical activity. Frequent screen use and exposure to violence during leisure time were also identified as concerns. Community LHT responses indicated differences between municipalities in perceptions of school meals, safety, and access to public services. Focus groups highlighted priorities concerning physical activity, school food environments, and coordination between schools, families, and the community. The findings indicate context-specific strengths and areas for further attention in child health and wellbeing. Quality of life, sleep patterns, and certain family health practices were generally favorable. Conversely, challenges were identified regarding physical activity, screen time, and psychological symptoms, as well as less favorable assessments of school meal quality, community safety, access to services, and opportunities for active leisure.

papers.title: A comparative evaluation of thiol/disulfide homeostasis and ischemia-modified albumin levels in patients with heroin use disorder in remission and detoxification.
papers.abstract: Chronic heroin use disturbs body's redox (oxidant-antioxidant) balance, together with dynamic thiol-disulfide balance and ischemia-modified albumin; which are two distinct blood markers that may reflect the oxidative and ischemic load in substance dependence. It is still unclear whether these markers change across the clinical phases of heroin use disorder (HUD), or whether they relate to the affective and behavioral symptoms that dominate the clinical picture. In this cross-sectional study, 101 adults meeting DSM-5 criteria for HUD were split into a remission group (n = 52) and a detoxification group (n = 49). We measured serum native and total thiol, disulfide, the disulfide/native thiol, disulfide/total thiol and native thiol/total thiol ratios, and IMA. Participants also completed a symptom inventory, a craving measure, and scales for healthy-lifestyle behavior and nutrition attitude. Groups were compared with Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney U test, categorical variables with chi-square or Fisher's exact test; associations were tested with Spearman correlations, and predictors of total thiol and IMA with multiple linear regression. Patients in detoxification group scored markedly higher on depression, anxiety, anger, somatic symptoms, suicidal ideation, psychosis, sleep disturbance, dissociation and craving (all p ≤ 0.001), and lower on healthy-lifestyle and nutrition-attitude scores (p < 0.001). In contrast, no thiol/disulfide measure or IMA differed between phases. IMA correlated positively with depression (r = 0.254) and craving (r = 0.209); whereas the disulfide/thiol ratios correlated negatively, and native thiol/total thiol positively with healthy-lifestyle and nutrition-attitude scores. Regression models for total thiol and IMA were not statistically significant. In HUD, redox and ischemia markers appear to follow symptom severity; especially depression, craving and health behavior, rather than the treatment phase itself. IMA, in particular, may reflect an oxidative and inflammatory component of mood regulation and craving.
